Indonesian law amendment sparks controversy. Xi Jinping makes rare visit to North Korea. Indian project endangers island tribe.

Iran: A series of escalating attacks between Iran and the United States threatened to upend their shaky ceasefire, as the White House insisted the two sides were “very close” to reaching a deal.

Iran said on Thursday it attacked US forces at bases in Kuwait and Bahrain following US strikes on sites in southern Iran and near the Strait of Hormuz – repeating a similar round of strikes 24 hours earlier.

The US said it had acted in self-defence and was responding to the downing of an Apache helicopter by an Iranian drone off the coast of Oman. Iran said the attack was an accident. The helicopter’s two crew members were rescued by a US drone boat.

Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said on social media: “Our Powerful Armed Forces will leave no attack or threat unanswered.”

The strikes followed a separate exchange of attacks on Sunday and Monday between Iran and Israel. Iran initially fired missiles at Israel, saying it was responding to Israel’s attacks on Hezbollah strongholds in Lebanon. Israel then responded with strikes on Iran, despite Donald Trump reportedly urging Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu not to retaliate.

Iran and Israel agreed this week to suspend attacks, though Iran warned it could launch further strikes should Israel attack Hezbollah, an Iran-backed group in Lebanon.

Clashes between Israel and Hezbollah continued this week, as Hezbollah launched rockets at Israel’s north and Israel attacked sites in southern Lebanon.

Despite the growing tensions across the region, US Vice President J.D. Vance said a deal that includes a long-term solution to Iran’s nuclear program could take days or months but was likely to be agreed before the US midterm elections in November. “I always hear people ask me, ‘Do you trust the Iranians?’ ” he told CBS News. “And what the president has said is: ‘I don’t trust anybody.’ ”

Indonesia: Police in Indonesia will be allowed to hold civil service posts under new legislation that has raised concerns about President Prabowo Subianto’s moves to expand the role of the security services in government.

The Indonesian parliament passed a bill on Tuesday allowing police to work in positions outside the police force as long as the jobs involve tasks related to policing. These jobs could include roles at ministries or state institutions that involve public security and safety.

Indonesia’s minister of law, Supratman Andi Agtas, said the police force needs to adapt to “increasingly complex security challenges”.

The new bill follows a separate law passed in 2025 that applied to the military and broadened the types of civilian posts that serving officers can hold.

Since becoming president in 2024, Prabowo, a former special forces commander, has expanded the role of the military and police in government, including involving them in the rollout of his program to provide free meals to children and pregnant women.

Rights groups have criticised the growing role of the security services, which have added to concerns the country’s democracy is gradually eroding.

Haeril Halim, of Amnesty International Indonesia, told Reuters the changes were “a sign of authoritarianism where defence and security forces are used to back those in power”.

North Korea: Chinese President Xi Jinping made a rare visit to North Korea this week, declaring the two countries “share a common destiny” as he tried to shore up relations with Pyongyang, which has been deepening ties with Russia.

During a meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, Xi, who was accompanied by his wife, Peng Liyuan, and was making his first international trip of the year, called for greater trade and closer military and diplomatic relations.

North Korea is China’s only formal ally but has been drawing closer to Moscow, particularly since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. North Korea has sent troops to fight for Russia – about 2300 are believed to have died – in return for Russian supplies of food and oil as well as weapons technology.

But analysts believe Xi has been concerned that North Korea’s ties with Russia could diminish China’s influence.

Kim assured Xi this week the relationship between the countries was “unbreakable”.

“Your choice of Pyongyang for the first overseas trip this year fully reflects the great importance you attach to … the profound friendship between the two countries, which is a tremendous encouragement to the [North Korean] side,” he said.

China opposes North Korea’s nuclear program – which could lead to Seoul and Tokyo seeking nuclear weapons – but has stopped making public calls for denuclearisation in recent years, possibly over concerns that pressuring Kim could lead to the regime’s collapse. Official Chinese and North Korean readouts of the talks between Xi and Kim this week did not mention nuclear arms.

India: Great Nicobar, a small Indian Ocean island covered by tropical rainforest, is one of the world’s most isolated inhabited places. The island belongs to India, despite being closer to Indonesia, Thailand and Malaysia, and is home to the indigenous Shompen people – one of the world’s last remaining largely uncontacted tribes – and indigenous Nicobarese people, as well as Indians from the mainland.

According to Indian data, 237 of the island’s residents are Shompen, 1094 are Nicobarese and 8000 are mainland Indians.

But the island, which is almost 1600 kilometres from the Indian mainland and has not been visited by an Indian prime minister for 42 years, is set to undergo a dramatic transformation.

The Indian government is proposing a US$9 billion development that will include construction of a civilian and military airport, a massive port for container ships, a power plant and a town and hotels that can host a million tourists a year.

The plan – called the Great Nicobar Project – seeks to “transform Great Nicobar into a strategic maritime and economic hub”, creating an Indian stronghold in the eastern Indian Ocean that could help to counter China’s regional rise.

Great Nicobar is only 40 nautical miles from the Strait of Malacca, which carries up to 30 per cent of total seaborne trade and is one of the world’s most crucial choke points.

But the project, due to cover a fifth of the island, has raised concerns it could threaten the indigenous people and cause widespread environmental damage.

Manish Chandi, who has researched the Nicobar archipelago, told NPR the project was “an open invitation to disaster”.

“It poses a threat to a huge amount of natural resources, its biological diversity and its indigenous communities,” he said.

India’s opposition leader, Rahul Gandhi, visited the island in April and described the project as “one of the biggest scams and gravest crimes against this country’s natural and tribal heritage in our lifetime”.

The government has insisted the project will avoid areas used by the Shompen people and will not threaten vulnerable flora and fauna. Construction began last year but is not due to be completed until 2047.

Barnabas Manju, the Nicobarese’s most senior leader, told AFP: “If we lose control of these lands, our culture too will be lost.”
